name: NVIDIA Rubin CPX
disclaimer: Illustrative geometry. Rubin CPX's exact die size and GDDR7 chip footprint are not published by NVIDIA; drawn to the same unit scale as other chips in this set using the TSMC reticle limit as a stand-in for die size (estimate). Memory chip count, SM grid and video/attention block counts are symbolic, not exact.

components.name: Package substrate
components.desc: Standard organic flip-chip substrate. Unlike NVIDIA's HBM parts, Rubin CPX needs no silicon interposer or CoWoS bridge: GDDR7 chips wire-bond straight to the substrate like a gaming GPU board, which is a big part of why this part is cheaper per GB than an HBM-equipped Rubin.

components.name: Rubin CPX compute die
components.desc: A single monolithic die — a deliberate break from Blackwell's two-die MCM. NVIDIA's slide emphasizes 'monolithic die design'; going single-die removes the die-to-die link entirely and simplifies yield math, at the cost of being capped by the reticle limit for total transistor budget. Holds SMs, L2, GDDR7 memory controllers, the attention-acceleration hardware and the video encode/decode engines.

specs.label: Die size
specs.value: Not published; drawn at the ~26×33 mm TSMC reticle limit used for the Blackwell die, as a size stand-in only

components.name: L2 cache
components.desc: On-die L2, shared by all SMs. During prefill it holds the full prompt's activations and the KV cache being built for the context window — the whole reason this part exists is to crunch through that prompt fast.

components.name: GDDR7 memory controllers
components.desc: GDDR7 PHY: fewer, faster pins per byte than an HBM PHY, so it costs less silicon and package area for a given capacity — the trade-off is lower aggregate bandwidth than HBM for the same GPU. That trade works for prefill because prefill re-uses the loaded prompt across a large compute-heavy matmul instead of re-reading weights once per output token.

components.name: Video encode/decode engines
components.desc: On-die NVENC/NVDEC blocks, reported at roughly 4x the video encode/decode throughput of a standard Rubin GPU. Lets Rubin CPX ingest and tokenize hour-long video directly on-chip for million-token multimodal context, without round-tripping frames through a separate CPU/GPU decode step.

specs.label: Video engines
specs.value: Integrated NVENC + NVDEC, ~4x a standard Rubin GPU's throughput (exact engine count not disclosed by NVIDIA)

components.name: PCIe 6.0 / scale-out fabric
components.desc: Rubin CPX trays reportedly lean on PCIe 6.0 for host and GPU-to-GPU links rather than a full NVLink-C2C fabric — another cost lever versus the HBM Rubin, which needs the fatter coherent fabric to move KV cache for decode.

components.name: SMs (bank A)
components.desc: Streaming Multiprocessors. Each SM carries Tensor Cores for NVFP4 matmuls plus the new hardware attention-acceleration path. The grid is symbolic — this model does not claim an exact SM count. Click **Open SM** to look inside.

components.name: GDDR7 chips (left bank)
components.desc: Discrete GDDR7 DRAM packages, surface-mounted directly on the substrate — no through-silicon-via stack, no HBM base die, no interposer. Cheaper per GB and per package than HBM, but each chip's own I/O is narrower, so the GPU needs many chips around the die to reach useful aggregate bandwidth. 128 GB announced, split across left and right banks here.

specs.label: Memory type
specs.value: GDDR7, not HBM — chosen because prefill is compute-bound, not bandwidth-bound

specs.label: Chip count / arrangement
specs.value: Drawn as 16 packages (8 left, 8 right); exact die-count per GPU not disclosed

components.name: GDDR7 chips (right bank)
components.desc: Second bank of GDDR7 packages, mirroring the left bank on the other side of the die.

components.name: L1 / Shared memory
components.desc: Programmable scratchpad shared by a block's threads. TMA fills it with Q/K/V and weight tiles; Tensor Cores and the attention unit both read operands straight from here.

specs.label: Size (per SM)
specs.value: ~256 KB (carried over from Blackwell-class SM design; Rubin's exact figure not published)

components.name: Tensor Memory (TMEM)
components.desc: Dedicated accumulator memory for Tensor Core MMAs, inherited from Blackwell's Tensor Memory design. Frees registers so larger NVFP4 tiles can be processed per instruction.

specs.label: Size (per SM)
specs.value: ~256 KB (Blackwell-class estimate; Rubin's exact figure not published)

components.name: Tensor Core
components.desc: Multiplies whole NVFP4 matrix tiles per instruction — the bulk of prefill's FFN and projection FLOPs. NVIDIA rates the GPU at up to 30 PFLOPS NVFP4; almost all of it is spent here during the compute-bound prefill pass.

components.name: Attention-acceleration unit
components.desc: Fixed-function hardware for the attention pattern itself — QK^T, softmax and the AV reduction — rather than running it as generic Tensor Core matmuls plus a softmax kernel. NVIDIA reports 3x the attention throughput of a GB300 NVL72 system; prefill's O(n²) attention cost over a million-token context is exactly the workload this block targets.

components.name: Register file
components.desc: Per-thread registers — the fastest storage, one slice per SM sub-partition.

components.name: Warp scheduler + CUDA cores
components.desc: Issues ready warps each cycle; scalar CUDA cores run the epilogue (bias, activation, quantization) after the Tensor Core and attention-unit results land.

components.name: TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator)
components.desc: Copies whole tensor tiles between L2/GDDR7 and shared memory asynchronously, without spending threads — same mechanism as Blackwell's TMA.

steps.text: 1. The prompt/context tokens and their weights sit in GDDR7, not HBM — cheaper per GB, and prefill doesn't need HBM-class bandwidth.

2. The GDDR7 memory controller reads activations and weights. GDDR7's narrower, slower interface is fine here: prefill is compute-bound, so the GPU is limited by FLOPs, not by how fast it can pull bytes.
3. Data lands in the shared L2 cache, which holds the whole prompt's activations and the KV cache being built as the context is processed.
4. TMA copies Q/K/V and weight tiles from L2 into shared memory, asynchronously.
5. Tiles sit in shared memory, ready for both the Tensor Cores and the attention unit.
6. The attention-acceleration unit runs QK^T, softmax and the AV reduction in hardware — 3x a GB300 NVL72 by NVIDIA's numbers — instead of emulating it with generic matmuls.
7. Tensor Cores multiply the FFN/projection tiles in NVFP4 — this is where most of the 30 PFLOPS announced for Rubin CPX is spent.
8. Partial sums accumulate in TMEM rather than in registers. Steps 4-8 repeat for every tile along the context length.
9. Epilogue: results move TMEM -> registers; CUDA cores add bias, apply activation, quantize back to NVFP4.

10. The finished KV cache writes back to GDDR7 and hands off over PCIe 6.0 to a separate HBM-equipped Rubin GPU for decode — which IS memory-bandwidth-bound, re-reading weights and KV cache once per output token, so it needs HBM instead.
11. For video/multimodal context, the on-die NVENC/NVDEC engines decode frames directly into tokens for prefill, at roughly 4x a standard Rubin's video throughput — no separate decode card needed.

summary.value: Not published; drawn at ~858 mm² (TSMC reticle limit, used as a size stand-in)
~800 W chip (~880 W module; SemiAnalysis estimate, not published by NVIDIA)
~20 PFLOPS dense NVFP4 (NVIDIA's 30 PFLOPS headline is the sparse figure; 3:2 ratio per SemiAnalysis)
~2 TB/s (estimate: 512-bit bus at ~32 Gbps GDDR7; not published by NVIDIA)
Standard organic substrate, no CoWoS/interposer (no HBM to route)

scale.basis: Die drawn at the ~26 x 33 mm TSMC reticle limit (Blackwell-class, used as a stand-in — Rubin CPX's real die size is not published); GDDR7 package ~4 x 3.6 mm footprint drawn per unit (estimate, not a real IC's exact pad size)
